description: We are a team of young Dominican women driven by science, technology, and innovation. Our multidisciplinary strengths span artificial intelligence, programming, data analysis, design, communication, and research. We combine diverse perspectives and expertise to transform ideas into practical, creative solutions for real-world challenges. We are committed to advancing meaningful innovation with positive global impact.
summary:
Farming Without Barriers is an AI virtual assistant linked to a repository of NASA satellite data (POWER, SMAP, GPM, and MODIS), complemented by a provincial survey on crops, production techniques, and the needs of farmers in each area.

It addresses the challenge by translating complex data on weather, soil moisture, and vegetation into clear guidance for planning harvests and preventing risks. To reach everyone, it offers three channels: a web platform, WhatsApp, and a telephone line (007), designed for those who struggle with digital tools. The assistant also educates: rather than just giving an answer, it teaches farmers to build their own knowledge.

It matters because scientific information only creates opportunities when it reaches the people who need it and they can understand it. The project does not replace farmers’ experience but complements it, building a bridge between space science and farming communities.
details:
FARMING WITHOUT BARRIERS was created with the purpose of bringing science and technology closer to the countryside by developing an artificial intelligence capable of transforming NASA satellite data, weather forecasts, and information collected directly from farmers into practical, personalized agricultural solutions. By analyzing the conditions of each plot of land, the AI will help identify planting opportunities, select suitable crops, and plan rotations that support soil conservation and water use. Our proposal aims to ensure that scientific information stops being complex or inaccessible and becomes a useful tool for those who work the land, regardless of their location or level of technological access.

The AI will integrate NASA satellite data, weather information, and national surveys of farmers. Its sources will include GPM, which provides rainfall estimates; SMAP, which measures soil moisture; and Terra and Aqua, whose MODIS sensors make it possible to observe changes in vegetation. This data will be combined with local information gathered through surveys on the needs and conditions of each area. The system will have two main modules: a weather forecasting module, which will analyze data and models to anticipate possible rainfall, temperatures, and droughts; and an agricultural planning module, which will use those forecasts, soil characteristics, and previous crops to recommend planting periods and rotation strategies.

Through an artificial intelligence and a broader, more interactive digital application, users will be able to consult information about their crops, learn new agricultural practices, and receive guidance tailored to their land and needs. In this way, we seek to reduce information limitations, drive the growth and development of the agricultural sector, and give farmers tools that allow them to learn, improve their practices, and make decisions with greater confidence.

Its main innovation will be making artificial intelligence accessible to farmers with different levels of literacy and technological access. They will be able to use it through a digital platform, WhatsApp, SMS, and phone calls, expanding its range of impact. It will also have a personalized technical assistance network with the numeric line 007. In the Dominican Republic, the support of the Ministry of Agriculture would be sought to offer free calls, connect queries with specialized technicians, and coordinate farm visits when necessary. The solutions obtained will be incorporated into the system’s knowledge base to improve future guidance. The goal is to provide access to more than 95% of the farmers in the communities where it is implemented.

At the international level, it will rely on a shared cloud technology infrastructure, while each country will have its own network of specialists and institutions. For example, in the Dominican Republic, the aim would be to collaborate with the Ministry of Agriculture and, in the United States, with the USDA and agricultural universities. This will allow the AI to be adapted to the languages, cultures, and agricultural conditions of each territory, avoiding generic recommendations that do not respond to local needs.

Although digital agriculture already exists in countries such as India, China, the United States, and Senegal, access to it remains unequal. For this reason, our proposal seeks to reduce that gap by bringing science and technology to more farming communities. Its feasibility rests on leveraging existing technologies and data, complemented by local knowledge and human assistance. In this way, HER ORBIT presents an innovative, adaptable, and relevant solution to improve agricultural decision-making at the local and international levels.
